articles.summary: 作者通过疫情期间团队在线玩密室逃脱游戏的经历，引出了关于“隐形问题”的讨论。在游戏中，每个人需要在各自的牢房中寻找线索，找到解决谜题的物件并组合起来才能逃脱。这隐喻了团队协作中那些不易察觉但需要共同发现和解决的问题。文章强调了识别和解决这些隐形问题对于团队成功的重要性。
articles.summaryEn: The author uses the experience of playing an online escape room game with the team during the pandemic to introduce a discussion on "invisible problems." In the game, each person had to find clues in their own cell and find objects to solve pieces of the puzzle to escape. This serves as a metaphor for those inconspicuous problems in team collaboration that require collective discovery and resolution. The article emphasizes the importance of identifying and solving these invisible problems for team success.
articles.reason: 以生动的密室逃脱隐喻揭示了团队协作中容易被忽视的“隐形问题”。

blocks.text: During the pandemic, we completed one of our largest projects at work. To celebrate, since we couldn't meet in person, we all ordered food on DoorDash and played an online escape room game together. We were on a Zoom call, helping each other out and having fun. The first challenge was to escape a jail cell.

To escape, each of us had to find clues in our own cell to figure out how to open the doors. We each had to find an object that solved a piece of the puzzle, and once we put them all together, the door would open. As a first challenge, it was easy enough. Everyone found a brightly colored object in their room and described it to the team so we could piece it together. Everyone but one team member.
"Come on, read it, man, we can win this."

He froze. Someone jumped in to help: "Mine was the most obvious green object in the room. Just look for something bright. Maybe blue, or orange, something that seems out of place." He didn't respond. He just sat there, frozen on camera. We figured he was having internet connectivity issues. We waited a good five minutes before he finally found it, and we moved on to the next level.

I didn't think much of that day. We finished the game, we had fun, it was great. He waited until our next one-on-one to explain what had actually happened. He panicked, and he was embarrassed. It turned out he was colorblind. We were yelling random color names at him, and he couldn't, for the life of him, see any of them.

As far as I can tell, I'm not colorblind, and it never would have occurred to me that this was something to account for. Just last week, I learned about Vehicle Motion Cues on the iPhone, a feature that helps reduce motion sickness. I don't think I've ever experienced motion sickness myself, or at least never in a car.

Watching a blind person navigate a website was eye-opening for me. I realized that many of my past design choices would have worked against their experience without my ever knowing it. The same goes for someone navigating a computer entirely by voice. I recently rediscovered Windows Speech Recognition, which I found pretty annoying for my own needs. But for someone who relies on it for all of their computer use, it's an essential tool.

A coworker once mentioned, almost in passing, that she struggles to read certain fonts because of dyslexia. Tight letter spacing and low-contrast text make some of our internal tools nearly unreadable to her. I had picked those fonts because they looked good on a demo slide. It had never crossed my mind that a font choice could be the difference between someone reading a document easily and someone giving up on it entirely.

In some of our zoom calls, a teammate would often ask if he could do audio only before the call. While it didn't bother me at all, the managers kept insisting on everyone turning on their cameras. But after he used the camera for a few minutes, his connection would start dropping. I just assumed he had slow Internet. But the reality was he was located in a rural area and he relied entirely on his phone's hotspot to connect to the internet. The zoom call was using up all his data in minutes.

None of these problems were problems for me. That's exactly what made them invisible. Unless you are experiencing these issues, there's little reason to ever notice them. We tend to design our tools, our meetings, and our expectations around our own experience of the world, and then mistake that experience for the default. It takes a colorblind teammate freezing on a call, or a friend who can't ride in the passenger seat without getting sick, to remind us that "normal" was only ever normal for us.

You can never anticipate every invisible problem in advance, that's impossible. But at the very least, we should remember that our own experience is rarely the default. We should be a bit more curious on how others experience the tools we build.

translations: 疫情期间，我们在工作中完成了最大的项目之一。为了庆祝，由于无法线下见面，我们都在 DoorDash 上点了餐，并一起玩了一个在线密室逃脱游戏。我们在 Zoom 通话中互相帮助，玩得很开心。第一个挑战是逃出一间牢房。
为了逃脱，我们每个人都必须在自己的牢房里寻找线索，弄清楚如何打开门。我们每个人都要找到一个能解开谜题一部分的物品，一旦我们把它们拼凑起来，门就会打开。作为第一个挑战，这相当简单。每个人都在自己的房间里找到了一个颜色鲜艳的物品，并向团队描述它，以便我们拼凑出完整的线索。除了一个团队成员，所有人都找到了。
“快点，读出来，伙计，我们能赢的。”
他愣住了。有人跳出来帮忙：“我的是房间里最显眼的绿色物品。找点颜色鲜艳的就行。也许是蓝色，或者橙色，看起来有些格格不入的东西。”他没有回应。他只是坐在那里，在镜头前僵住了。我们以为他的网络连接出了问题。我们足足等了五分钟，他才终于找到了，然后我们进入了下一关。
那天我并没有多想。我们完成了游戏，玩得很开心，感觉很棒。他一直等到我们下一次一对一沟通时，才解释了到底发生了什么。他当时很慌张，也很尴尬。原来他是色盲。我们冲他喊着各种颜色的名字，而他无论如何也看不到任何颜色。
据我所知，我并不是色盲，我也从未想过这是需要考虑的因素。就在上周，我了解到了 iPhone 上的“车辆运动提示”功能，这是一个有助于减轻晕车的功能。我觉得我自己从来没有晕过车，或者至少在车里从来没有过。
看着盲人浏览网站让我大开眼界。我意识到，我过去的许多设计选择在不知不觉中阻碍了他们的体验。对于完全依靠语音操作电脑的人来说也是如此。我最近重新发现了 Windows 语音识别功能，我觉得它对我自己的需求来说相当烦人。但对于完全依赖它来使用电脑的人来说，这是一个必不可少的工具。
一位同事曾经几乎是不经意地提到，由于患有阅读障碍，她很难阅读某些字体。紧凑的字间距和低对比度的文本使得我们的一些内部工具对她来说几乎无法阅读。我当初选择那些字体只是因为它们在演示幻灯片上看起来不错。我从未想过，字体的选择可能会决定一个人是轻松阅读一份文档还是完全放弃阅读。
在我们的一些 Zoom 通话中，一位队友经常在通话前询问是否可以只使用语音。虽然我完全不介意，但经理们一直坚持要求每个人都打开摄像头。但当他打开摄像头几分钟后，他的连接就会开始掉线。我只是以为他的网速很慢。但事实是，他住在农村地区，完全依靠手机热点连接互联网。Zoom 通话在几分钟内就会耗尽他所有的流量。
这些问题对我来说都不是问题，而这正是它们变得不可见的原因。除非你亲身经历这些问题，否则几乎没有理由去注意它们。我们往往根据自己对世界的体验来设计工具、安排会议和设定期望，然后误将这种体验视为默认标准。直到有色盲的队友在通话中卡住，或者有朋友一坐副驾驶座就晕车，才会提醒我们：“正常”其实只是对我们而言才正常。
你永远无法提前预见到每一个不可见的问题，那是不可能的。但至少，我们应该记住，我们自身的体验很少能代表默认标准。我们应该对他人如何体验我们所构建的工具多一点好奇心。

articles.title: Book Review: The Field Guide to Understanding 'Human Error' by Sidney Dekker ★★★★☆
articles.titleZh: 书评：Sidney Dekker 的《理解“人为错误”实地指南》
articles.summary: 这篇书评介绍了 Sidney Dekker 的著作，该书认为所谓的“人为错误”实际上并不存在。大多数灾难是由系统问题、激励错位和不切实际的流程引起的，而不是人类自身的不可靠。读者并非安全系统的守护者，不需要保护系统免受不稳定人类的影响。虽然内容略显重复，但它为学生和从业者提供了重新审视事故归因的有用视角。
articles.summaryEn: This book review introduces Sidney Dekker's work, which argues that there is no such thing as "human error." Most catastrophes are caused by system issues, misaligned incentives, and unrealistic processes, rather than human unreliability. You are not the custodian of an otherwise safe system that needs protection from erratic human beings. Although a bit repetitive, it provides a useful perspective for students and practitioners to re-examine accident attribution.
articles.reason: 颠覆了对“人为错误”的传统认知，为系统设计和事故分析提供了全新的视角。

blocks.text: This is such a useful book. It makes the case that there's no such thing as "human error" - instead most catastrophes are caused by system issues, misaligned incentives, and unrealistic processes.
You are not the custodian of an otherwise safe system that you need to protect from erratic human beings.
By its nature it is a little repetitive. I suspect it's the sort of book students and business leaders will be expected to dip into on an ad-hoc basis for their MBA studies.

It's also chock-full of anecdotes which demonstrate how quite serious failings are often erroneously reduced to "human failure". Some of those stories are rather distressing - featuring death, dismemberment, plane crashes, and the like - but they also feel a little like "just so" stories. They illustrate the points well, but felt to me a little voyeuristic.
I'd go so far as to say it is probably one of the best management books that I've read:
I'm a big fan of using bullet-points for books like this. It is far too easy for important insights to get buried in the middle of a paragraph of waffle.
And it isn't just for management types. Anyone involved in computers needs to read and understand this.
new technology allows a system to be driven closer to its margins, eroding the safety advantage that was gained.
Although it doesn't venture into politics and government, I think it also applies there. Consider this:
What people were doing was reasonable in the eyes of those on the inside the situation, given the pressures and priorities operating on them and others doing the same work every day.

Modern political discourse often implies that decision makers are incompetent buffoons who frequently make errors. I think the truth is rather closer to what the book suggests. Given all the information (which the commentariat rarely have) and the systemic incentives (which are often set by the electorate) - most decisions look reasonable from the inside. A more systems based view rather than hindsight analysis would be useful for everyone.
There are a few slightly naff clip-art illustrations which are probably better suited to a crappy PPT than a serious book.

It is also a pity the eBook is so malformed. The HTML is full of things like

rather than using proper semantic headers, which means the built in style-sheet must be used, which means you can't easily change the default font colour (dark grey on eInk looks rubbish). I'd love to see some of the tools and techniques proposed in this book applied to the organisation which created this rather terrible formatting.
The author is extremely generous with his citations and points to hundreds of resources for readers to explore.
A worthwhile book for anyone who deals with even moderately complex systems - if you can put up with the error-riddled formatting.

translations: 这是一本非常有用的书。它论证了不存在所谓的“人为错误”——相反，大多数灾难是由系统问题、激励错位和不切实际的流程造成的。
你并不是一个原本安全的系统的看护者，不需要去保护它免受反复无常的人类的破坏。
就其本质而言，这本书有些重复。我怀疑它属于那种学生在 MBA 学习期间会被要求临时翻阅的书，商业领袖也是如此。
书中还充满了各种轶事，展示了相当严重的失误是如何经常被错误地归结为“人为失误”的。其中一些故事相当令人痛苦——涉及死亡、肢体残缺、空难等——但它们也让人觉得有点像“本来如此”的故事。它们很好地说明了观点，但在我看来有点窥探隐私的感觉。
我甚至想说，这可能是我读过的最好的管理学书籍之一：
追究人们的责任是可以的；• 但你需要能够证明，人们拥有履行你现在要求他们承担的责任的权力；• 如果你做不到这一点，你要求问责的呼吁就毫无意义，你最好开始审视自己。
我非常喜欢在这类书中使用项目符号。因为重要的见解太容易被埋没在冗长啰嗦的段落中间了。
而且它不仅仅适合管理阶层。任何从事计算机工作的人都需要阅读并理解这本书。
新技术使得系统可以被推向其极限边缘，从而侵蚀了原本获得的安全优势。
虽然它没有涉足政治和政府领域，但我认为它同样适用于那里。考虑一下这一点：
考虑到他们以及每天从事同样工作的其他人所面临的压力和优先事项，在处于局内的人看来，他们的所作所为是合理的。
现代政治话语经常暗示决策者是无能的蠢货，经常犯错误。我认为事实更接近于这本书所暗示的那样。考虑到所有信息（评论员很少拥有）和系统性激励（通常由选民设定）——大多数决策从内部来看都是合理的。一种更基于系统的视角，而不是事后诸葛亮式的分析，对每个人都会很有用。
书中有一些略显俗气的剪贴画插图，它们可能更适合糟糕的 PPT，而不是一本严肃的书。

电子书的格式如此糟糕也很令人遗憾。HTML 中充斥着

这样的标签，而不是使用正确的语义标题，这意味着必须使用内置样式表，也就意味着你无法轻易更改默认字体颜色（在 eInk 上深灰色看起来糟透了）。我很想看到这本书中提出的一些工具和技术，被应用到制造了这种糟糕排版格式的组织身上。
作者在引用文献方面非常慷慨，为读者指出了数百种可供探索的资源。
对于任何处理哪怕只是中等复杂系统的人来说，这都是一本值得一读的书——前提是你能忍受充满错误的排版格式。

blocks.text:
Marcus Hutter—oldheads will remember him from AIXI—recently
published a book: Job-Less Utopia: Macroeconomics in the Age of
AGI.  I’m always curious what the people building AI think or want the
future to look like, and I’m also always looking for non-doomer takes on the
post-AGI future, so I decided to read it and review it.

The first thing to say is that nearly every sentence is written by AI. To his
credit, Hutter says so plainly:

Claude also served as the most diligent editor I could have hoped for: While I
have a reasonable grasp of economic concepts, I am neither a professional
economist nor a native English speaker, so it was invaluable to have someone
polish my clumsy English into professional language. No text was taken
verbatim without my critical review, revision, and approval.

Like many people who use AI to write, he uses this tiresome “I’m not a native
English speaker 🥺” argument. But he published an English-language book
in 2005—which I read!—and it was infinitely more readable than this. Now, I
suspect Claude did more than just editing, because the book is full of
unnecessary and convoluted figures, tables, abbreviations, taxonomies, including
(and I swear to God this is verbatim from the book):

“a Wittgensteinian property-cluster definition of ‘job’ (11 properties × 8
edge cases)”
“a formal job–leisure spectrum showing how UBI degrades job properties”
“a four-camp taxonomy of positions on automation”

“A technology-level taxonomy (five cognitive AI levels plus two robotic
levels) is mapped onto a job-replacement matrix showing what threshold
automates 10%, 50%, 90%, and 99% of each occupation (Table 3.3).”

Which is exactly the kind of make-work cognitive dreck that LLMs love to write
to pass the time. As a result the book is unpleasant, confusing, verbose,
repetitive slop.

So, going forward, I’ll be treating Claude as the author. Sorry Marcus! Make
something real next time. Now, Claude’s argument is simple: AGI and robotics,
which are said to be inevitable, will take all our jobs, and we can tax the
vastly increased economic output to create widespread prosperity. Most of the
book is about the economic realizability of taxing AGI wealth and paying out
UBI.

The main problem with the book is the signal-to-noise ratio. Most of it is
obvious. Other than “AGI and robotics will take ~all jobs”, which is of course
uncertain, everything else is uncontroversial: yes, output in the jobless AGI
world would increase rather than decrease; yes, the surplus can be taxed to
provide UBI; yes, we still need money even in the jobless utopia to coordinate
economic activity. There’s some stuff about self-replicating machines I already
know: we’ve all read Drexler and Freitas here. You don’t need
260 pages to explain all this. The one part that is semi-novel is this idea of
using Pigouvian taxes to disincentivize so-called “bullshit
jobs”. God, I hate Graeber so much.

There’s an interesting bit about intellectual property. Claude’s argument here
is that AGI plus present-day IP law would lead to a massive concentration of
wealth, while simultaneously “the traditional justification for IP
(incentivizing human creativity through temporary monopoly) weakens markedly
once AI systems generate the bulk of patentable inventions and copyrightable
works at near-zero marginal cost”. The solutions: shorter patent terms,
Harberger taxes, compulsory patent licensing. So, as part of the
transition to the job-less utopia, the whole world will have to coordinate to
essentially abolish IP. Which seems very hard. I doubt the Disney corporation
will go gently into that good night.

The most interesting questions around AGI are not economic, but rather questions
of political economy. For example: if most humans become materially and
economically useless, how do they maintain a political voice? That is: how do we
preserve democracy when the state no longer needs its people? Claude admits this
is a problem, e.g. on page 132:

The “Age of Labor” conferred unprecedented political power on workers (Korinek
and Stiglitz, 2021); they could strike, withhold their contribution, and
thereby constrain employers and governments (Boix, 2019). Full automation
extinguishes this lever entirely: if no human labor is needed, a strike is
merely self-imposed privation. UBI restores livelihood but not agency over
production.
And page 141:

The economics are tractable in principle (Chapter 3), but translating them
into policy requires political will, social cohesion, and a credible answer to
the search for meaning in a post-labor world. When redistribution fails, the
consequences range from populism to regulatory capture and a transition-period
underclass risk, yet democratic feedback loops nonetheless incentivize
corrective action (Section 7.1 and Figure 7.1). A deeper structural question
follows: if the state no longer depends on citizen labor for economic output,
does the democratic social contract survive?

Alright. What’s the solution? There’s a lot of verbiage, most of which is
self-undermining. For example:

Deterrence and the social contract.

  Although the ruling class’s reliance on citizen labor in time led to
democracy, losing this reliance will not necessarily cause democracy to
collapse. As long as the population can physically revolt against dismantling
democracy, and threaten the comfortable lifestyle of those in power, the
incumbents have an incentive to avoid a civil war. This is perhaps the only
good (among many arguably bad) argument for the right of individuals to own
firearms: civilian arms serve as a credible last-resort deterrent against
state tyranny, the practical embodiment of the revolution threat that formal
models identify as the historical driver of democratic concessions (Boix,
2019).  However, this deterrent erodes rapidly once autonomous weapons and
robotic enforcement become available, allowing a regime to suppress revolt
without relying on potentially sympathetic human soldiers (see Table 7.2, row
“Military dependence”). The deterrence argument is genuinely contested.

In other words: “the people can revolt, wait, no, they can’t, because autonomous
weapons—uhhh it’s contested”. Alright, so physical deterrence doesn’t
work. What else?

The preceding sections painted a sobering picture, but the historical record
is not uniformly grim. Democracies have absorbed structural shocks of
comparable magnitude before, and institutional innovations ranging from direct
democracy to sortition offer structural resistance to oligarchic capture.

It is obviously not true that “democracies have absorbed structural shocks of
comparable magnitude before”. Nothing remotely like AGI or ASI has happened in
human history, let alone the history of modern democracies.

This is followed by a bunch of smoke-and-mirrors misdirection about various
“democratic innovations” that could keep the state in check. But Claude is just
shuffling the papers here, because, ultimately, why does it matter what words
you write on a piece of parchment? The material reality is unchanged: the humans
in this “job-less utopia” will be economically useless, physically disarmed, and
under constant surveillance. Why would they have political power?

There’s a bit about the resource curse, which I will quote because it
highlights the low standard of reasoning in the book, and how LLMs are more than
happy to construct sophistical, self-undermining arguments on command, with no
concern for truth or sound argumentation:

The theoretical mechanism behind the resource curse is clean: (i) government
funded by resource rents no longer needs citizen taxes; (ii) no taxation
erodes accountability (“no taxation, no representation”); (iii) citizens lose
leverage and democratic institutions atrophy. But empirically, the mechanism
is less airtight than it appears. The United States funded itself primarily
through tariffs for its first 150 years without democratic collapse; many
non-democracies tax heavily (the Soviet Union, China); and the mechanism
assumes that fiscal dependence is citizens’ only source of leverage, whereas
labor power, military service, and sheer numbers have historically mattered at
least as much.

You see what I mean? Tariffs are a terrible example, because tariff revenue is
not decoupled from labour in a world where all economic activity is human
activity. Then there’s the arguments about “labor power, military service, and
sheer numbers”. Labour power? The whole point of the book is that:

The advent of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and advanced robotics will
eventually permanently decouple economic productivity from human labor.

What labour power? Furthermore, how do “military service” and “sheer numbers”
give people political power, in a world where states have autonomous weapons and
AI-enabled mass surveillance?
The key political economy questions here are:

How will the citizens, who are economically useless, preserve any political
voice at all?
How will people in countries other than the US benefit from AGI?

And neither is answered satisfactorily. Besides, there are questions of social
organization that the book either grazes or doesn’t touch at all:

How do intellectually talented people distinguish themselves when AGI does all
intellectual activity?

What happens to society when life outcomes become independent of character
traits, when the responsible and the irresponsible are equally rewarded? Do we
want to live in such a world?

Today, the human competitive drive is vented as positive-sum
entrepreneurship. In the post-labour world, where does this go? League of
Legends? Politics, war? What happens to society when human activity is reduced
to zero-sum status war?
Finally, I found this sentence ironic:

AI sharply lowers the cost of [content pollution], threatening to flood the
information ecosystem with synthetic low-value content at a scale that
overwhelms human curation.

translations: Marcus Hutter——资深人士可能还记得他提出的 AIXI——最近出版了一本书：《无业乌托邦：AGI时代的宏观经济学》。我总是很好奇那些构建 AI 的人是怎么想的，或者希望未来是什么样子，我也一直在寻找关于后 AGI 未来的非末日论观点，所以我决定读一读并写篇书评。
首先要说的是，几乎每一句话都是 AI 写的。值得称赞的是，Hutter 坦率地承认了这一点：
Claude 也充当了我所能期望的最勤奋的编辑：虽然我对经济学概念有较好的掌握，但我既不是专业经济学家，也不是英语母语者，因此能有人将我笨拙的英语润色成专业语言，其价值不可估量。任何文本都没有在未经我批判性审查、修改和批准的情况下逐字照搬。
像许多使用 AI 写作的人一样，他用了这套令人厌倦的“我不是英语母语者🥺”的说辞。但他在 2005 年出版过一本英文书——我读过！——那本书的可读性比这本强无数倍。现在我怀疑 Claude 所做的不仅仅是编辑，因为这本书充满了毫无必要且错综复杂的图表、表格、缩写和分类法，其中包括（我向上帝发誓这是书里的原话）：
“‘工作’的维特根斯坦式属性簇定义（11个属性 × 8个边缘情况）”
“一个展示 UBI 如何削弱工作属性的正式工作-休闲光谱”
“关于自动化立场的四阵营分类法”
“一种技术层面的分类法（五个认知 AI 层级加上两个机器人层级）被映射到工作替代矩阵上，展示了何种阈值能自动化每个职业的 10%、50%、90% 和 99%（表 3.3）。”
这正是 LLMs 为了打发时间而喜欢写的那种凑字数的认知垃圾。结果就是，这本书成了一堆令人不快、令人困惑、冗长且重复的粗制滥造之物。
因此，接下来我将把 Claude 视为本书作者。抱歉了 Marcus！下次弄点真东西吧。现在来说，Claude 的论点很简单：据称不可避免的 AGI 和机器人将夺走我们所有的工作，而我们可以对大幅增长的经济产出征税，从而创造广泛的繁荣。这本书的大部分内容都在探讨对 AGI 财富征税并发放 UBI 的经济可行性。

这本书的主要问题在于信噪比太低。大部分内容都显而易见。除了“AGI 和机器人将取代几乎所有工作”这一点尚不确定之外，其他所有内容都毫无争议：是的，在无业 AGI 世界中，产出会增加而不是减少；是的，盈余可以被征税以提供 UBI；是的，即使在无业乌托邦中，我们仍然需要货币来协调经济活动。还有一些关于自我复制机器的内容，这些我早就知道了：我们这里都读过 Drexler 和 Freitas 的著作。你根本不需要用 260 页来解释这一切。唯一算得上半点新意的是，利用庇古税来抑制所谓“狗屁工作”的想法。天哪，我真是太讨厌 Graeber 了。

关于知识产权有一个有趣的论点。Claude 在这里的论点是，AGI 加上当前的知识产权法将导致财富的大规模集中，同时“一旦 AI 系统以接近零的边际成本生成了大部分可申请专利的发明和受版权保护的作品，知识产权的传统正当性理由（通过临时垄断来激励人类创造力）就会显著减弱”。解决方案包括：缩短专利期限、征收哈伯格税（Harberger taxes）、强制专利许可。因此，作为向无工作乌托邦过渡的一部分，全世界必须协调起来，从根本上废除知识产权。这似乎非常困难。我怀疑迪士尼公司会轻易地接受这种结局。
围绕 AGI 最有趣的问题不是经济问题，而是政治经济学问题。例如：如果大多数人在物质和经济上变得毫无用处，他们如何维持政治话语权？也就是说：当国家不再需要其人民时，我们如何维护民主？Claude 承认这是一个问题，例如在第 132 页：
“劳动时代”赋予了工人前所未有的政治权力（Korinek 和 Stiglitz，2021）；他们可以罢工、拒绝提供劳动，从而制约雇主和政府（Boix，2019）。全面自动化彻底消除了这一杠杆：如果不需要人类劳动，罢工仅仅是自我剥夺。全民基本收入（UBI）恢复了生计，但并没有恢复对生产的控制权。
以及第 141 页：
原则上，经济问题是可解决的（第 3 章），但将其转化为政策需要政治意愿、社会凝聚力，以及对后劳动时代意义探索的可靠回答。当再分配失败时，后果从民粹主义到监管俘获以及过渡期底层阶级风险不等，然而民主反馈循环仍然会激励纠正行动（第 7.1 节和图 7.1）。随之而来的一个更深层次的结构性问题是：如果国家不再依赖公民劳动来获取经济产出，民主社会契约还能存续吗？
好吧。解决方案是什么？文中有很多辞藻，其中大部分都在自我拆台。例如：

威慑与社会契约。尽管统治阶级对公民劳动的依赖最终促成了民主，但失去这种依赖并不一定会导致民主崩溃。只要民众能够在物理上反抗对民主的瓦解，并威胁到当权者的舒适生活方式，在位者就有动机避免内战。这也许是支持个人拥有枪支权利的唯一好论点（在许多可以说是糟糕的论点之中）：平民武装是对抗国家暴政的可靠最后威慑手段，是正式模型所认定的民主让步的历史驱动力——即革命威胁——的实际体现（Boix，2019）。然而，一旦自主武器和机器人执法成为可能，这种威慑就会迅速瓦解，使得政权在镇压叛乱时不再依赖可能产生同情的士兵（见表 7.2，“军事依赖”行）。威慑论点确实存在争议。
换句话说：“人民可以反抗，等等，不，他们不能，因为自主武器——呃，这存在争议”。好吧，那么物理威慑不起作用。还有什么办法？
前面几节描绘了一幅令人清醒的画面，但历史记录并非全然黯淡。民主制度以前也曾吸收过同等规模的结构性冲击，而从直接民主到抽签制等各种制度创新，为抵御寡头篡权提供了结构性的阻力。
“民主制度以前曾吸收过同等规模的结构性冲击”这显然是不对的。在人类历史上，甚至根本没有任何事物能像 AGI 或 ASI 那样发生过，更不用说在现代民主制度的历史中了。
接下来是一堆关于各种能够约束国家的“民主创新”的障眼法和误导。但 Claude 在这里只是在玩弄文字游戏，因为归根结底，你在一张羊皮纸上写下什么字真的有那么重要吗？物质现实并没有改变：在这个“无工作的乌托邦”中，人类在经济上将毫无用处，在物理上被解除武装，并处于持续的监控之下。他们凭什么会有政治权力？
书中有一点关于资源诅咒的内容，我将引用它，因为它突显了书中低下的推理标准，以及 LLMs 是多么乐于在指令下构建诡辩的、自我拆台的论点，而毫不关心真相或严密的论证：

资源诅咒背后的理论机制很清晰：(i) 由资源租金提供资金的政府不再需要公民纳税；(ii) 不纳税会侵蚀问责制（“无代表不纳税”）；(iii) 公民失去筹码，民主制度萎缩。但在经验上，这个机制并不像看起来那样无懈可击。美国在其前150年主要依靠关税筹集资金，却没有发生民主崩溃；许多非民主国家征税很重（苏联、中国）；而且该机制假设财政依赖是公民唯一的筹码来源，而历史上劳动力、服兵役和纯粹的人数至少同样重要。
你明白我的意思了吧？关税是一个糟糕的例子，因为在所有经济活动都是人类活动的世界里，关税收入并没有与劳动力脱钩。然后是关于“劳动力、服兵役和纯粹的人数”的论点。劳动力？这本书的全部要点是：
通用人工智能（AGI）和先进机器人的出现，最终将使经济生产力与人类劳动力永久脱钩。
哪来的劳动力？此外，在一个国家拥有自主武器和 AI 驱动的大规模监控的世界里，“服兵役”和“纯粹的人数”如何赋予人们政治权力？
这里的关键政治经济学问题是：
在经济上毫无用处的公民，将如何保留任何政治发言权？
美国以外国家的人将如何从 AGI 中受益？
这两个问题都没有得到令人满意的回答。此外，还有一些社会组织问题，这本书要么一笔带过，要么根本没有触及：
当 AGI 承担了所有的智力活动时，有智力天赋的人如何脱颖而出？
当生活结果不再取决于性格特征，当有责任心的人和不负责任的人得到同样的回报时，社会会发生什么？我们想生活在这样一个世界里吗？
今天，人类的竞争动力通过正和的创业活动得到释放。在后劳动力世界里，这会走向何方？League of Legends？政治、战争？当人类活动沦为零和的地位战争时，社会会发生什么？
最后，我发现这句话很讽刺：
AI 大幅降低了[内容污染]的成本，威胁着要用海量的合成低价值内容淹没信息生态系统，其规模之大足以压垮人工筛选。

articles.summary: Welcoming the Nepalese Government to Have I Been Pwned

blocks.text: Today, we welcome the 47th government onboarded to Have I Been Pwned’s free gov service: Nepal. Their National Cyber Security Centre now has access to monitor Nepalese government domains against the data in HIBP. This gives the NCSC the ability to identify exposure across government email addresses and respond quickly when those accounts appear in a new data breach.

This is precisely what the HIBP government service was built for: helping national cyber teams strengthen threat monitoring and incident response capabilities by providing visibility into compromised credentials and breached accounts across their government domain space.

Nepal joins a growing list of governments and national cybersecurity teams using HIBP to better understand their exposure, protect government departments and public resources, and reduce the risk posed by compromised credentials before attackers can take advantage.

blocks.text: Yesterday I wrote that a lot of the special functions that pop up in mathematical physics are solutions to second order linear differential equations with polynomial coefficients. More generally, holonomic functions are defined to be those functions that are the solutions to linear differential equations, of any order, with polynomial coefficients.

Most special functions are holonomic. To quantify that statement, I went through the special functions covered in Abramowitz and Stegun. The large majority are holonomic, thought some common functions like the gamma function are not holonomic.

This report goes through the functions in A&S. For those that are holonomic, it gives the differential equation that the function solves. The large majority of these equations are second order, but not all. And the coefficients are nearly always first or second order polynomials, rarely higher order.

articles.title: ★ Why Apple Requires a Cellular Account Through a Big Three Carrier to Lease an iPhone
articles.titleZh: ★ Why Apple Requires a Cellular Account Through a Big Three Carrier to Lease an iPhone
articles.summary: ★ Why Apple Requires a Cellular Account Through a Big Three Carrier to Lease an iPhone

blocks.text: Following up from last week, when I asked:

When you lease an iPhone through Apple Upgrade, you need a
cellular account on one of the big three U.S. carriers: AT&T,
T-Mobile, or Verizon. That kind of stinks, and I’m not quite sure
I understand why. You’re leasing the iPhone through Apple and
Klarna, not the carrier, so I don’t know why Apple cares. If you
know why, shoot me a message and explain it. Is it just a
simplistic credit-risk evaluation, where prepaid plan-holders and
MVNO users in general are viewed suspiciously?

I got a slew of messages about this. Credit-risk assessment is seemingly part of it. There’s a lot of fraud in iPhone purchases specifically and cell phone service generally. The big three carriers do a significant amount of risk assessment before letting you open a new postpaid account; that you have an active account with one of them is a signal that you’re not trying to lease an iPhone using phony credentials in order to sell it.

But the bigger reason is the complex nature of the contracts between Apple and each of the big three carriers. A reader who worked on the carrier team at Apple for a long time (but left a few years ago) wrote:

In response to your question on why Apple would only offer iPhone
on the “Big 3” for the new Upgrade Program: Every year, the
Carrier Teams at Apple negotiate a deal/program (hundreds of
millions of dollars) with each of those Big 3. In return for those
dollars, Apple will make concessions exactly like this (or
similar.) This is also why, for example, their logos appear more
prominently or are the only ones called out on signage,
commercials, etc… Although they really aren’t threatened by MVNO’s
(the ones they don’t own) or regional carriers, it’s more like
Apple is selling it as part of a package deal that’s exclusively
offered to its biggest and best “tier 1” partners. It also acts as
a carrot to perpetually try to motivate smaller partners into
behavior Apple wants.

This might change — some of the bigger MVNOs are trying to work their way into “tier 1” (or maybe create a new “tier 1.5”). But for many years now, part of the co-marketing agreements between Apple and the Big Three is Apple agreeing to require a postpaid account with a Big Three carrier for all “special” iPhone financing deals, including the old iPhone Upgrade Program and the new Apple Upgrade leasing.

One interesting exception is that Boost Mobile is included alongside the Big Three for Apple Card Monthly Installments (ACMI), a program that offers 0% APR on certain products if you pay for them using an Apple Card. From the ACMI small print:

In order to buy an iPhone with ACMI, you must select one of the
following carriers (prepaid carrier plans are not supported):
AT&T, Boost Mobile, T-Mobile, or Verizon. An iPhone purchased with
ACMI is always unlocked, so you can switch carriers at any time,
subject to your carrier’s terms.
So perhaps some of the bigger MVNO carriers might work their way into Apple Upgrade — but if they do, it sounds like they’ll need to pay Apple for the privilege.
With regard to fraud, a former Apple Store retail employee wrote:

I left in 2019, but I’d estimate on some days a double digit
percentage of in-person phone sales were fraudulent.

This behavior absolutely exploded when you started to be able to
do carrier financing in the store. They had stolen the identity
of a legit account holder, come into the store with the info
needed to access the account. They always wanted the highest end
phone, and would pay the sales tax due at time of sale in cash.
Never wanted any accessories. Never wanted to open the box or set
up the phone.

As bad as it was with the activation requirement, it would be way
worse without it. I believe it’s gotten a lot better, and the
carriers have more advanced systems in place to detect and deter
this behavior now. But ultimately, the carriers ate the cost for
millions of dollars in devices they never got paid for.
I suspect that reader is correct that Apple, in collaboration with the carriers, has cracked down on this.

translations: 接续上周的话题，当时我问了这样一个问题：

当你通过 Apple Upgrade 租赁 iPhone 时，你需要拥有美国三大运营商之一（AT&T、T-Mobile 或 Verizon）的蜂窝网络账户。这有点让人不爽，我也不太明白为什么会这样。你是通过 Apple 和 Klarna 租赁 iPhone，而不是通过运营商，所以我不知道 Apple 为什么会在意。如果你知道原因，请发消息给我解释一下。难道这仅仅是一种简单的信用风险评估，认为预付费套餐用户和 MVNO 用户通常比较可疑吗？
我收到了大量关于这个问题的留言。信用风险评估似乎确实是原因之一。在购买 iPhone 以及一般的手机服务中，存在大量的欺诈行为。三大运营商在允许你开设新的后付费账户之前，会进行大量的风险评估；你在其中一家拥有活跃账户，这本身就是一个信号，表明你不是想用虚假身份租赁 iPhone 然后倒卖。
但更大的原因在于 Apple 与三大运营商之间合同的复杂性。一位曾在 Apple 运营商团队工作多年（但几年前已离职）的读者写道：

关于你提出的为什么 Apple 在新的 Upgrade Program 中只向“三大”运营商提供 iPhone 的问题：每年，Apple 的运营商团队都会与这三大运营商分别谈判一项交易/计划（价值数亿美元）。为了换取这些资金，Apple 会做出类似这样的（或类似的）让步。这也是为什么，例如，他们的标志会显示得更显眼，或者成为标牌、广告等中唯一被提及的运营商……尽管他们实际上并没有受到 MVNO（非其旗下的）或区域性运营商的威胁，但这更像是 Apple 将其作为一项独家提供给其最大且最好的“一级”合作伙伴的打包交易的一部分。它也起到了一种激励作用，不断促使较小的合作伙伴采取 Apple 所期望的行为。
这种情况可能会改变——一些较大的 MVNO 正试图跻身“一级”（或者可能创建一个新的“1.5级”）。但多年来，Apple 与三大运营商之间的联合营销协议中，有一部分是 Apple 同意要求所有“特殊”的 iPhone 融资交易（包括旧的 iPhone Upgrade Program 和新的 Apple Upgrade 租赁）都必须拥有三大运营商的后付费账户。
一个有趣的例外是，在 Apple Card Monthly Installments (ACMI) 计划中，Boost Mobile 与三大运营商一起被列入其中。该计划规定，如果你使用 Apple Card 支付某些产品，可享受 0% 的年利率。ACMI 的附属细则中写道：
为了使用 ACMI 购买 iPhone，你必须选择以下运营商之一（不支持预付费运营商套餐）：AT&T、Boost Mobile、T-Mobile 或 Verizon。使用 ACMI 购买的 iPhone 始终处于解锁状态，因此你可以随时更换运营商，但需遵守你所在运营商的条款。
因此，也许一些较大的 MVNO 运营商可能会设法进入 Apple Upgrade——但如果他们真的这么做，听起来他们需要向 Apple 支付这笔“入场费”。
关于欺诈问题，一位前 Apple Store 零售店员工写道：

我是在2019年离职的，但我估计在某些日子里，实体店手机销售中有两位数百分比是欺诈性的。当门店开始能够办理运营商分期付款时，这种行为简直呈爆炸式增长。他们盗取了合法账户持有人的身份，带着访问该账户所需的信息来到店里。他们总是想要最高端的手机，并且会在购买时用现金支付应付的消费税。从不想要任何配件。从不要求开箱或设置手机。尽管有激活要求的情况已经很糟了，但如果没有这个要求，情况会更糟。我相信现在情况已经好多了，运营商也部署了更先进的系统来检测和阻止这种行为。但最终，运营商承担了数百万美元从未收到过付款的设备成本。
我怀疑那位读者说得对，Apple 已经与运营商合作，对这种行为进行了严厉打击。

articles.title: Truth Social Launches Paid Early Access to Trump Posts
articles.titleZh: Truth Social Launches Paid Early Access to Trump Posts
articles.summary: Truth Social Launches Paid Early Access to Trump Posts

blocks.text:
President Donald Trump holds up a copy of his Truth Social post about Air Force One as he speaks with the media aboard Air Force One on July 8, 2026. The president's media company is offering investors early access to his Truth Social feed for up to $100,000 a month, raising ethical and legal concerns.
                
                    
                    Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption
toggle caption
Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
President Trump, his critics like to say, learned one major lesson during his first term: Never leave any money on the table.
But even for a president who raked in $2 billion, fueled mostly by his lucrative cryptocurrency ventures, the latest offering from his social media platform, Truth Social, stands out.
Trump Media & Technology Group is now shopping to traders and investors a premium version of Truth Social delivering early access to the feeds of high-profile users, including the president.

Starting Saturday, for a fee of up to $100,000 a month, trading firms can access "Truth API" to get a glimpse of the president's often market-moving announcements about economic policy and global affairs before the rest of the world.

Trump's media company says customers have already started signing up. Such an offering would give institutional investors a leg up in areas of finance like high-frequency trading, where an advantage of a few milliseconds can mean the difference of millions of dollars. But will the service be widely adopted across Wall Street?

"It's insane," said one Wall Street executive, who requested anonymity for fear of retaliation from the Trump administration. "I can say for myself and 200 of my friends in finance, we're not getting anywhere near this. In another administration, this would be considered criminal."

NPR reached out to 12 other major players in finance, brokers, hedge fund managers and other investors. None would speak publicly about the service, with some saying the risk of landing in Trump's crosshairs was too high.
Former SEC official says Truth API appears illegal
Securities experts, however, are drawing attention to the legal concerns surrounding the service.
Renée Jones, a Boston College professor and former top official at the Securities and Exchange Commission, said the paid offering appears to run afoul of insider trading laws.

She pointed to federal securities laws prohibiting schemes in which non-public information is misused to give a trader an unfair advantage. The law states that sharing such information is a breach of "a duty or trust of confidence."

"So if the president's Truth Social posts are being monetized, and if some people get special access to them, that's misappropriated information," Jones said. "And by giving people his posts early, he is also violating his duty of trust and confidence."

Offering specialized data access to paying customers is not unusual or illegal for social media companies. But given that Trump regularly announces or hints at official government policy via Truth Social, the paid service could quickly run into legal problems, according to Jones.
She pointed to the 2012 Stock Act, which prohibits members of Congress and the executive branch, including the president, from trading stocks based on privileged information.
"That said, I could imagine Trump's lawyers arguing that because they announced it out in the open, it's not deceitful, it's not fraudulent," Jones said.
Shannon Devine, a spokeswoman for Trump Media & Technology Group, said in a statement that offering an early preview of posts from the president and others does not amount to insider trading.

"Truth API offers customers the fastest way to ingest publicly available Truth Social data. Critics must have invented a new theory of 'insider trading' based on publicly available information," Devine said.
Democratic Senators demand SEC investigation
Democratic Senators have called on federal regulators to probe whether Truth API is indeed breaking securities law.

In a letter sent Wednesday to the SEC by Sens. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Adam Schiff of California, the lawmakers called the service "an outrageous abuse of the President's office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets." They asked the commission to launch an investigation.
The SEC declined to comment.
Trump Media & Technology Group spokeswoman Devine dismissed the letter as partisan wrangling.

"With no apparent sense of irony, certain politicians falsely accuse us of anti-free-market behavior while pressuring businesses into boycotting a product, all in a coordinated effort to harm a publicly traded company," Devine said.
Trump is the largest shareholder of his media company through a trust controlled by his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., regulatory filings show.
That means the Trump family's wealth will grow as customers sign up for Truth API.
It's the latest example of the president blurring the lines between public office and his business empire.

"Channeling nonpublic information to Trump's media company for high-speed dissemination to his wealthy institutional investors is a step toward normalizing insider trading that undermines the integrity of U.S. markets and further erodes investor confidence," said Virginia Canter, a former SEC lawyer who is now with Democracy Defenders Fund, a nonprofit that has been critical of the Trump administration.
Canter added that the product "disadvantages regular investors who unfortunately may be on the losing sides of those trades because they do not have the same access to information."

特朗普总统的批评者常说，他在第一个任期内学到了一个重要教训：绝不放过任何赚钱机会。
但即使对于一位通过利润丰厚的加密货币项目狂赚20亿美元的总统来说，其社交媒体平台 Truth Social 的最新产品也显得格外引人注目。
特朗普媒体科技集团目前正向交易员和投资者推销 Truth Social 的高级版本，该版本提供对包括总统在内的高知名度用户动态的提前访问权。
从周六开始，交易公司只需每月支付高达10万美元的费用，即可访问“Truth API”，从而在全世界其他人之前，抢先看到总统经常能引发市场波动的关于经济政策和全球事务的声明。
特朗普的媒体公司表示，客户已经开始注册。这样的产品将使机构投资者在金融领域（如高频交易）中占据优势，在这些领域，几毫秒的优势可能意味着数百万美元的差距。但这项服务会在整个华尔街被广泛采用吗？
“这太疯狂了，”一位华尔街高管表示，由于担心遭到特朗普政府的报复，他要求匿名。“我可以代表我自己和金融界的200位朋友说，我们绝对不会碰这个。如果在其他政府执政期间，这会被认为是犯罪。”
NPR 联系了金融界的另外12位主要参与者，包括经纪人、对冲基金经理和其他投资者。没有人愿意公开谈论这项服务，一些人表示，成为特朗普打击目标的风险太高了。
前美国证券交易委员会（SEC）官员称 Truth API 似乎违法
然而，证券专家们正在引起人们对围绕该服务的法律担忧的关注。
波士顿学院教授、前美国证券交易委员会高级官员雷内·琼斯表示，这项付费服务似乎违反了内幕交易法。
她指出了联邦证券法禁止滥用非公开信息以使交易员获得不公平优势的方案。法律规定，分享此类信息构成了对“受托责任或信任义务”的违背。
“因此，如果总统的 Truth Social 帖子被变现，并且如果某些人获得了对这些帖子的特殊访问权，那就是被挪用的信息，”琼斯说。“通过提前向人们提供他的帖子，他也违反了自己的信任和保密义务。”
对于社交媒体公司来说，向付费客户提供专门的数据访问权并不罕见，也不违法。但琼斯指出，鉴于特朗普经常通过 Truth Social 宣布或暗示官方政府政策，这项付费服务可能会很快遇到法律问题。
她提到了2012年的《停止利用国会知识交易法案》（Stock Act），该法案禁止国会和行政部门（包括总统）成员基于特权信息进行股票交易。
“话虽如此，我可以想象特朗普的律师会辩称，因为这是公开宣布的，所以它不是欺骗性的，也不是欺诈性的，”琼斯说。
特朗普媒体与科技集团的发言人香农·迪瓦恩在一份声明中表示，提前预览总统及其他人的帖子并不构成内幕交易。
迪瓦恩说：“Truth API 为客户提供了获取公开 Truth Social 数据的最快途径。批评者一定是基于公开信息发明了一种新的‘内幕交易’理论。”
民主党参议员要求 SEC 展开调查
民主党参议员呼吁联邦监管机构调查 Truth API 是否确实违反了证券法。
在马萨诸塞州参议员伊丽莎白·沃伦和加利福尼亚州参议员亚当·希夫周三致 SEC 的一封信中，议员们称该服务“为了个人利益而滥用总统职权，损害了普通投资者的利益和市场的完整性，令人愤慨”。他们要求该委员会展开调查。
SEC 拒绝置评。
特朗普媒体与科技集团发言人迪瓦恩将该信件斥为党派争端。
迪瓦恩说：“某些政客显然毫无讽刺感，他们一边诬陷我们存在反自由市场行为，一边又向企业施压要求抵制某款产品，这一切都是为了协同损害一家上市公司。”
监管文件显示，特朗普通过其长子小唐纳德·特朗普控制的信托，成为其媒体公司的最大股东。
这意味着随着客户注册使用 Truth API，特朗普家族的财富将会增长。
这是总统模糊公职与其商业帝国界限的最新例证。
弗吉尼亚·坎特曾是一名 SEC 律师，现就职于一直对特朗普政府持批评态度的非营利组织“民主捍卫者基金”。她表示：“将非公开信息引导至特朗普的媒体公司，以便高速分发给其富有的机构投资者，这是使内幕交易正常化的一步，损害了美国市场的完整性，并进一步削弱了投资者的信心。”
坎特补充说，该产品“让普通投资者处于劣势，不幸的是，由于他们无法获得同等的信息，可能会在这些交易中处于亏损的一方。”
一位要求匿名的华尔街高管问道：“他应该能够像这样将总统职位变现吗？我不这么认为。但投资银行会为此冒风险吗？可能不会。”
